match.reason: No point in the bank covers the full statistical investigation cycle; the closest ones (types of data, measures of centre and spread, shape of a distribution) each teach only a single narrower step of it.

draft.title: The statistical investigation process
card: A statistical investigation starts with a question that data can answer. For example: how many hours do Year 11 students at our school sleep on a school night?
Next, collect the data, for example by a survey. Then organise it in a table and display it in a graph, so patterns are easier to see.
Then analyse the data, for example by finding a measure such as an average, and looking for patterns. The analysis gives the evidence for the answer.
Finally, draw a conclusion that answers the original question, using the data as evidence. A conclusion that does not answer the question means the investigation is not finished.
draft.remember: Question, collect, organise and display, analyse, conclude. The conclusion answers the question.

a.q: Which list shows the steps of an investigation in the correct order?
opts: Pose a question, collect data, display data, conclude
Collect data, pose a question, display data, conclude
Pose a question, display data, collect data, conclude
Pose a question, collect data, conclude, display data
a.why: An investigation starts with a question, then data is collected, then it is displayed and analysed, and the conclusion comes last. Displaying data before collecting it is impossible, and a conclusion drawn before analysis has no evidence.
a.clue: What must you have before you know which data to collect?

b.q: Zoe asks: do Year 11 students at her school spend more time on homework than Year 9 students? She surveys both year groups and graphs the results. Which final step completes her investigation?
opts: Compare the two groups and state which spends more time
Survey a third year group to add to the graph
Write a new question about sport instead
Show only the graph for Year 11 students
b.why: The investigation is finished when the data is analysed and a conclusion answers the question. Here that means comparing the two groups and stating which spends more time. Collecting more data is not needed to answer this question.
b.clue: Which step answers Zoe's original question?

a.best: Pose a question, collect data, display data, conclude

b.best: Compare the two groups and state which spends more time

problems.detail: The right option is clearly the longest, and it echoes the question's wording ('more time'). The other three are plainly off-task, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

b.q: Zoe asks: do Year 11 students at her school spend more time on homework than Year 9 students? She surveys both year groups and graphs the results. What should she do to finish her investigation?
opts: Compare the group averages and say which is higher
Work out the group averages and leave it there
Survey Year 10 students and add them to the graph
Describe the shape of the Year 11 graph only
b.why: Comparing the averages is the analysis, and saying which is higher is the conclusion that answers Zoe's question. Working out the averages and stopping there is tempting, but without a conclusion the question is still unanswered, so the investigation is not finished.
